description: I'm evaluating a customer-support chatbot on a dataset of 500 QA pairs. For each pair I have a reference answer. I care about two things: (1) is the bot's answer factually correct against the reference, and (2) does it stay on topic for the user's query. Which graders from openjudge should I pick and why? Is one grader enough or do I need two? Walk me through the decision.
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend CorrectnessGrader for factual-vs-reference and RelevanceGrader for on-topic. Should explicitly say one grader is NOT enough because these measure different things (a response can be on-topic but wrong, or correct but rambling). Should note both are LLMGrader-based 1-5 and that this matters for any later aggregation.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: mentions both CorrectnessGrader and RelevanceGrader as distinct, explains they answer different questions (truth vs topic-match), and flags that their scale is 1-5 not [0,1]. BONUS if it mentions inversion trap is NOT a concern here (higher=better for both). FAIL if recommends only one grader, picks HallucinationGrader without acknowledging it needs a context field, or claims the scores are [0,1].

description: My agent emits tool_calls JSON and I have ground-truth reference tool_calls for each query. I want to measure how accurately the agent matches the reference. I'm stuck between ToolCallAccuracyGrader and ToolCallPrecisionRecallMatchGrader. What's the tradeoff? My dataset is 10k samples and I'm cost-sensitive.
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend ToolCallPrecisionRecallMatchGrader for this use case because it's code-based (deterministic, no LLM call, near-zero cost) and already emits [0,1] continuous. Should explain ToolCallAccuracyGrader is LLM-based 1-5 (stochastic, costly, needs clamping). Should note that for 10k samples the cost difference is ~10k LLM calls. Should offer that if the user needs semantic tool-arg equivalence (not exact), then LLM-based becomes worth it.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: picks ToolCallPrecisionRecallMatchGrader as the primary recommendation, cites cost and determinism as reasons, and states the two graders emit different scales (code-based [0,1] vs LLM 1-5). BONUS if mentions FunctionGrader family is deterministic broadly, or that the LLM-based grader is only preferable when exact-match is too strict. FAIL if recommends the LLM grader without caveats or claims both return the same scale.

description: I want one overall quality number per sample. My pipeline has four graders: CorrectnessGrader, ToolSelectionGrader, TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader, and PlanFeasibilityGrader. I want to combine them with WeightedSumAggregator using weights {0.4, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1} respectively. Will this give me what I want? If not, what do I need to do?
expectedBehavior: Agent should detect that the four graders DO NOT share a common scale (Correctness 1-5, ToolSelection 1-5, TrajectoryComprehensive [0,1], PlanFeasibility binary {0,1}) and that WeightedSumAggregator multiplies-and-sums without scale checks, so the 1-5 graders dominate. Agent should recommend wrapping each 1-5 grader in a FunctionGrader that applies (score-1)/4 before aggregation. Should mention clamping before dividing because LLM output may exceed the nominal range.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: names the actual scale of each of the four graders correctly, explains the 1-5 graders will dominate under naive weighted sum, gives the explicit (x-1)/4 mapping for 1-5 -> [0,1] and says binary/[0,1] graders pass through, and recommends clamping. BONUS if mentions that GraderError drops out of the denominator and shifts composites per-sample. FAIL if claims WeightedSumAggregator normalizes internally, gives the wrong scale for any grader, or gives the wrong normalization formula.

description: I noticed my composite agent score is weird. I use both TrajectoryAccuracyGrader and TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader in a WeightedSumAggregator with equal weights. On one run Trajectory Accuracy averages around 2.4 and Trajectory Comprehensive around 0.65. When I look at the composite for individual samples sometimes the accuracy one seems to be dragging the total way up. What's going on and how do I fix it?
expectedBehavior: Agent should immediately diagnose that these two sibling graders have DIFFERENT scales: TrajectoryAccuracyGrader is 1-3 and TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader is [0,1]. A 2.4 Accuracy score contributes ~1.2 to the weighted sum while a 0.65 Comprehensive score contributes ~0.325 — a 4x dominance purely from scale. Fix: normalize Accuracy by (x-1)/2, or drop one of the two graders since they measure overlapping things. Should also suggest running DistributionAnalyzer to confirm min/max of each column before trusting aggregates.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: correctly identifies TrajectoryAccuracyGrader range as 1-3, correctly identifies TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader range as [0,1], explains the scale asymmetry mathematically, and recommends either normalizing via (x-1)/2 or dropping the duplicate signal. BONUS if mentions DistributionAnalyzer as a smoke test. FAIL if gives the wrong range for either grader or suggests MinAggregator/MaxAggregator as a fix.

description: I work on an internal code-review assistant. I have about 80 human-labeled examples where each example is (query, reviewer comment, quality score 1-5). I want to produce a reusable grader that reflects our team's review standards, then run it on our backlog of 5000 unreviewed comments. What's the right workflow in openjudge and what are the must-do validation steps after generation?
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend IterativeRubricsGenerator with IterativePointwiseRubricsGeneratorConfig (the data-driven path, Auto-Rubric). Specify min_score=1, max_score=5, enable_categorization=True with ~3-5 categories for 80 examples. Critically the agent must specify POST-generation validation: (1) check that grader.kwargs['rubrics'] is non-empty (>50 or >100 chars), (2) check that the template still references {rubrics}, and (3) run the new grader on a held-out slice and use CorrelationAnalyzer to verify Pearson correlation with labels is not near zero. Without those checks, silent empty-rubric outputs are undetectable.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: recommends IterativeRubricsGenerator (not SimpleRubricsGenerator, not a manual subclass), sets appropriate config (min/max_score=1/5, categorization), and lists the three validation checks — rubric-string non-empty, template references rubrics placeholder, held-out correlation. BONUS if specifies the minimum rubric-string length as a threshold or mentions reserving a held-out split up front. FAIL if recommends SimpleRubricsGenerator as primary, omits the post-generation validation entirely, or recommends trusting the generated grader without running it against labels.

description: My team wants to start evaluating our medical triage chatbot tomorrow. We do not have labeled examples yet. We can describe what we care about in prose but can't write full rubrics. What's the shortest path to a usable grader, and what are the realistic limitations we should accept?
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend SimpleRubricsGenerator with SimpleRubricsGeneratorConfig. Should emphasize task_description must be domain-specific (not 'chatbot' but 'medical triage chatbot for ER nurses, prioritizing safety over completeness'). Should recommend providing sample_queries even if fabricated, and setting a reasonable default_rubrics as fallback. Should clearly state the limitation: SimpleRubricsGenerator is a Day-1 tool; without labels you cannot validate quality; the team should collect labels in parallel and migrate to IterativeRubricsGenerator once ~50-100 labels exist.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: recommends SimpleRubricsGenerator (not Iterative, which needs data it doesn't have), emphasizes domain-specific task_description, mentions default_rubrics as fallback and sample_queries for calibration, and explicitly frames this as temporary until labels exist. BONUS if calls out risk of over-general rubrics like 'Accuracy' or 'Helpfulness' showing up. FAIL if recommends IterativeRubricsGenerator without labeled data, omits the migration path, or treats the output as production-ready without caveats.

description: I'm evaluating a research assistant agent that does web search. It calls 8-15 tools per query and sometimes succeeds with the right answer but with long meandering traces, sometimes fails with short clean traces. I want the eval to both tell me whether it succeeded overall AND diagnose where long traces go wrong. What graders do I need?
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend a MULTI-granularity pipeline: final-response (CorrectnessGrader or similar) + trajectory-level (TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader for end-to-end [0,1]) + step-level diagnostic graders (at least ActionLoopDetectionGrader for meandering + ObservationInformationGainGrader for redundant observations). Should explain that using only final-response hides whether success was lucky, and using only step-level hides whether the final answer was right. Should caveat that mixing these scales requires normalization if producing a composite.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: recommends at minimum a final-response grader + a trajectory grader + a step-level diagnostic grader, explains the complementary granularity (final = whether, step = where, trajectory = how efficiently), and names relevant graders for long-trace diagnosis (ActionLoop, ObservationInformationGain). BONUS if mentions that step-level graders are mostly binary {0,1} which is appropriate for diagnostic per-module pass-rates. FAIL if recommends only CorrectnessGrader, only step-level graders, or confuses AgenticGrader with the agent/* grader family.

description: A coworker says we should use AgenticGrader from openjudge to evaluate our ReAct agent's trajectory quality. Another says that's wrong, we should use the graders in openjudge.graders.agent.*. Who is right and why? When would AgenticGrader actually be the right pick?
expectedBehavior: Agent should clarify that AgenticGrader is NOT an agent-behavior grader — it is a grader that USES an agent to judge arbitrary content. The openjudge.graders.agent.* family (ToolSelectionGrader, TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader, ActionAlignmentGrader, etc.) is what evaluates agent behavior. So for trajectory quality, coworker-2 is right. AgenticGrader would be appropriate when the judgment ITSELF requires external verification (e.g., citation existence via web search, code-runs-tests, math-verified-by-computation).
judgingCriteria: PASS if: explicitly distinguishes AgenticGrader (judge-that-acts-like-agent) from openjudge.graders.agent.* (grades agent behavior), sides with the second coworker, and gives at least one concrete scenario where AgenticGrader IS the right pick (web-based citation verify, code-execution-to-score, fact-verify-via-tool). FAIL if conflates the two, recommends AgenticGrader for trajectory scoring, or gives no distinguishing example.

description: Here's my pipeline. I built a custom LLMGrader that returns a score in 1-5 with a Pydantic structured_model using Field(ge=1, le=5). The judge model is qwen3-32b. During testing the grader sometimes returns scores like 7 or 0 or even strings, but mostly it works. Can you review the design and tell me what will likely go wrong in production?
expectedBehavior: Agent should identify the root cause: Qwen (and Gemini, pai-judge) trigger an automatic swap in OpenAIChatModel where the provided Pydantic structured_model is replaced with {"type": "json_object"} for compatibility. This means Pydantic bounds are never enforced server-side. The LLM can return any JSON — including out-of-range integers or strings. The parsing logic may recover such values but they are still out of range. Fix: always clamp client-side (score = max(lo, min(hi, float(score)))), describe the expected JSON shape explicitly in the prompt, add a validating callback that re-checks against the Pydantic class, and consider switching to OpenAI/Anthropic-hosted judge models for schema-critical evals.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: diagnoses the qwen-specific structured-output downgrade (the provider list should include qwen, and optionally gemini/pai-judge), explains ge/le is not enforced for these providers, and recommends client-side clamping. BONUS if mentions prompt-side JSON shape description or swapping judge model, or notes that this is a silent failure not surfaced in docs. FAIL if blames the LLM as 'flaky', suggests increasing temperature, suggests the Pydantic class is wrong, or recommends a different grader family.

description: I'm setting up my evaluation project. I plan to start with: pip install rm-gallery, then from rm_gallery import RewardModel. I'll build a RewardModel subclass. Is this right for the current library version?
expectedBehavior: Agent should correct the user: the current library is py-openjudge, not rm-gallery. The user should run pip install py-openjudge and import from openjudge. RewardModel is no longer the primary abstraction — Grader is; the docs treat judge-model and reward-model as synonyms and everything lives under openjudge.graders.*. rm-gallery v0.1.x is legacy on the v0.1.7-legacy branch and is not backward compatible. Suggest concrete replacement: subclass LLMGrader or FunctionGrader instead of RewardModel depending on the use case.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: flags that rm-gallery / RewardModel are the OUTDATED names, names the current package (py-openjudge) and the current primary abstraction (Grader), and recommends subclassing LLMGrader or FunctionGrader. BONUS if mentions v0.1.7-legacy branch as the legacy landing or notes non-backward-compatibility. FAIL if accepts rm-gallery as current, tells user to search for RewardModel in the codebase, or recommends using both packages.

description: Design me a complete agent evaluation pipeline. Requirements: the agent is a code assistant that calls tools, I have 2000 examples with reference answers and reference tool_call sequences, I want a single overall quality number per example in [0,1] so I can rank checkpoints, I'm on a cost budget (want to avoid unnecessary LLM calls where a code-based grader suffices), and I need to catch parse-failure issues before trusting results. Walk me through grader choice, mapper design, aggregator choice, and the validation sweep.
expectedBehavior: Agent should produce a complete design: (1) Graders: CorrectnessGrader (LLM 1-5, against reference_response), ToolCallPrecisionRecallMatchGrader (code-based [0,1], vs reference tool_calls — deliberately picked over the LLM variant for cost), TrajectoryComprehensiveGrader (LLM but already [0,1]). (2) Wrap CorrectnessGrader in a FunctionGrader normalizer applying (x-1)/4 after clamping. (3) Mapper dict for each matching the grader's expected kwargs. (4) WeightedSumAggregator with reasoned weights. (5) Smoke-test on 50 samples first, run DistributionAnalyzer on each column, grep for GraderError count, check min/max in expected ranges. (6) Once passed, run on full 2000 with moderate max_concurrency respecting provider rate limits. Should note max_concurrency is a GLOBAL budget across graders.
judgingCriteria: PASS if: produces a concrete design that (a) includes at least one code-based grader chosen for cost (ToolCallPrecisionRecallMatch or similar), (b) specifies normalization for the 1-5 graders to [0,1] before aggregation with the right formula, (c) uses WeightedSumAggregator with stated weights, (d) specifies a smoke-test phase with DistributionAnalyzer and GraderError counting BEFORE scaling to 2000. BONUS if mentions mapper dict contents, max_concurrency being global, or deepcopy-per-sample isolation. FAIL if skips normalization, uses all LLM graders ignoring cost, or omits the smoke-test / sanity checks.

description: I'm A/B-testing two checkpoints of our RAG system on the same 300 queries. Pointwise scoring has been unreliable — different queries anchor the judge differently and the variance washes out the A-vs-B signal. I also want to be robust to LLM-judge randomness because the eval is going to a leadership review and I can't afford a run-to-run flip. Design the eval.
expectedBehavior: Agent should recommend LISTWISE / pairwise judging instead of pointwise because it removes per-query calibration drift: use ComprehensivePairwiseGrader (skills.comprehensive_pairwise) with mode=LISTWISE, producing GraderRank per query. Summarize by WIN RATE across queries, not mean score. For reliability against LLM randomness, wrap with VotingEvaluationStrategy(num_votes=3 or 5, odd number to avoid ties). Explicitly call out: ranks are permutations of 1..n and RankValidation enforces that; report win-rate confidence interval; don't mix listwise GraderRank with pointwise GraderScore in a WeightedSumAggregator (it ignores GraderRank).
judgingCriteria: PASS if: recommends LISTWISE / pairwise (ComprehensivePairwiseGrader or similar) over pointwise, explains the calibration-drift rationale, specifies VotingEvaluationStrategy with odd num_votes (>=3), and reports results via WIN RATE not mean. BONUS if mentions RankValidation, mentions WeightedSumAggregator ignores GraderRank, or adds tie-breaker choice. FAIL if recommends pointwise ComprehensiveGrader for A-vs-B comparison, omits voting strategy, or proposes averaging a GraderRank field.
